transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-07-31 16:00 PDT · 52 minutes · Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Sofia Martinez (Redwood SE), Priya Kapoor (Head of ML, HelixAI), Daniel Cho (Platform Engineer), Lucia Park (Security), Arjun Mehta (SRE)

[00:00] Jordan Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for joining—I'll kick off. This is Jordan from Redwood, with Sofia on the technical side. Can folks introduce themselves quickly?
[00:06] Priya Kapoor: Hi, Priya here, Head of ML at HelixAI. We're looking to validate Redwood for inference scale.
[00:10] Daniel Cho: Daniel, platform eng; I'm focused on capacity and cost.
[00:13] Lucia Park: Lucia, security. I will drive SOC2/KMS questions.
[00:17] Sofia Martinez: Great, thanks. Quick agenda: align on success criteria, go over baseline vs burst sizing, autoscale mechanics, and the benchmark plan.
[00:25] Jordan Lee: High level, HelixAI wants a POC to prove we can handle their chat workload with decent latency and predictable costs. Priya, can you share the SLOs you care about?
[00:34] Priya Kapoor: Sure. We're targeting p50 under 200ms and p95 under 900ms for a median chat with ~150 tokens response. Throughput needs to be 40 qps sustained, with spikes to 120 qps for several minutes. Quality mustn't degrade more than a 3% metric on our eval prompts.
[00:51] Sofia Martinez: That's helpful. So two levers: reserved GPUs for the sustained 40 qps, and a burst pool to absorb spikes up to 120 qps. We'll size reserved to meet baseline and autoscale into burst on demand.
[01:05] Daniel Cho: What instance types are you assuming? We are looking at A100 and maybe cheaper 80GB or even 4090 options. Also need to see cost delta for reserved vs on-demand bursts.
[01:17] Sofia Martinez: For initial POC we'd suggest 2x A100 reserved to hit baseline for medium-size models (7B-13B class) — that typically gives ~40–60 qps depending on sequence length and batch config. Burst could be up to +4 GPUs in a burst pool, either reserved spare or cloud burst. We can also route to quantized 4-bit variants to increase throughput if needed.
[01:38] Priya Kapoor: What's the startup time when autoscaling adds GPUs? Say we hit 120 qps, how fast do you ramp?
[01:44] Sofia Martinez: Good question. Cold-start for a new GPU instance and model warmup can be 60–180 seconds depending on image pull and model loading. To mitigate, we recommend a warm warm-pool or prewarmed models in standby for fast bursts — that's the burst strategy. Also cache KV prefix can reduce token work for repeated contexts.
[02:02] Arjun Mehta: Our patterns show spikes of 3–8 minutes. So 2–3 minute startup is acceptable if burst pool covers the head. But we care about fallback if we can't provision extra capacity.
[02:10] Jordan Lee: For fallback we typically implement model-variant fallback + regional fallback. Example: if primary is 13B fp16, we fallback to a quantized 13B or a 7B variant with config that preserves output format. That keeps latency bounded while degrading quality gracefully.
[02:25] Priya Kapoor: We need to define quality guardrails — if fallback is used, we want to log and surface to users. Also tie into evals so we measure delta.
[02:33] Sofia Martinez: Absolutely. We'll include quality telemetry in the benchmark. We'll capture p50/p95 latency, tokens/sec, GPU utilization, KV cache hit rate, and qualitative eval scores vs test prompts.
[02:45] Daniel Cho: On autoscale policy: what thresholds do you recommend? CPU isn't the best metric. GPU utilization, request queue length, or latency percentiles?
[02:53] Sofia Martinez: We recommend hybrid: primary triggers based on request queue depth and 95th latency crossing a threshold for a short window (e.g., p95 > 750ms for 30s) plus a queue length > X. Cooldown of ~90–180s to avoid flapping. Prefill warm pools when trend detection predicts spikes.
[03:12] Jordan Lee: Important point — reserved capacity reduces cost variance and gives predictable throughput. For POC we can propose two purchase options: small reserved commitment for baseline and a priced burst allowance for extra hours, or fully on-demand with a larger cost but no commit.
[03:28] Priya Kapoor: We need concrete numbers to compare. Also, what about multi-region? We may route to EU for some users.
[03:34] Sofia Martinez: We can support regional routing. For POC we'll focus in us-west, but can enable a secondary region for failover. That will affect costs and latency.
[03:44] Lucia Park: From security perspective: we require KMS integration for model artifacts and keys, SSO (SAML/Okta), and audit logs for inference requests. How do you handle customer-managed keys?
[03:54] Jordan Lee: Redwood supports KMS/HSM integrations and can accept customer-managed encryption keys for private deployments; for hosted POC we can set up a customer KMS connection. We'll include SOC2 artifacts and an architecture diagram for logging.
[04:05] Lucia Park: Also need data residency options and retention policy for logs. We want 90-day logs in-house and longer cold storage explicit.
[04:12] Jordan Lee: Noted. We'll include retention config and options in the docs.
[04:16] Priya Kapoor: For the benchmark, what inputs do you need from us?
[04:19] Sofia Martinez: We need sample traces, target QPS, distribution of sequence lengths, typical prompt templates, and eval prompt set for quality checks. Ideally 1–2 weeks of tps/requests to model traffic.
[04:29] Daniel Cho: I can pull traces. We'll sanitize and share. Note our traffic has mid-day spikes and nightly batch jobs that hit the model for summarization.
[04:38] Sofia Martinez: Great — include batch vs interactive separation. Batch workloads can be scheduled on cheaper backends or lower-priority pools. That informs autoscale policies.
[04:46] Priya Kapoor: Another ask: can you run a comparative bench between 13B fp16 and 13B 4-bit quant in the POC? We want to see latency/cost/quality tradeoffs.
[04:55] Sofia Martinez: Yes, we'll run side-by-side benchmarks and provide quality delta on your eval prompts. We'll also provide guidance on quantization profiles we recommend.
[05:03] Arjun Mehta: How do you measure cost-per-1000-requests or cost per token? We need that to present to finance.
[05:08] Jordan Lee: We'll provide cost modelling in the SOW: reserved amortized cost + burst hours + per-token or per-request unit economics. We'll produce a sample cost spreadsheet showing cost per 1k requests under baseline and spike scenarios.
[05:20] Priya Kapoor: Good. On timelines, we want a 4-week POC: week 1 configuration and security review, week 2 benchmark runs, week 3 analysis and tuning, week 4 wrap and decision. Is that realistic?
[05:29] Sofia Martinez: Yes, that's reasonable. If we get traces and approvals quickly we can start infra in 3–5 business days.
[05:36] Daniel Cho: Do you need network/VPC peering for the POC? Our infra is in a private VPC.
[05:40] Jordan Lee: For private deployment we'd do VPC peering or private network connections; for hosted POC we can support connector agents and secure egress. We'll include both options in the SOW.
[05:49] Lucia Park: Who owns logs for request payloads? We want token-level logs redacted for PII.
[05:54] Sofia Martinez: Redwood can redact and filter logs. For POC we'll align on redaction rules and a minimal set of fields retained.
[05:59] Priya Kapoor: Any risks you see?
[06:02] Sofia Martinez: Main risks: underestimating startup time for cold GPUs, burst pricing surprises if many bursts happen, and quality regressions with quantized fallbacks — we'll mitigate with warm pools, scheduled bursts, and guarded fallbacks that record quality metrics.
[06:16] Jordan Lee: Ok let me recap: 2x A100 reserved baseline, burst pool up to +4 GPUs (options: reserved spare vs cloud burst), autoscale based on queue/p95, cooldown ~90–180s, fallback to quantized/7B model with telemetry and guarded rollouts, security: KMS + SAML + audit logs, timeline 4 weeks with benchmark window in week 2. We'll send a SOW and benchmark template.
[06:39] Priya Kapoor: That matches our expectations. Please highlight the cost comparisons for reserved vs on-demand and include multi-region impact.
[06:46] Daniel Cho: Also include a runbook for how we initiate a surge and how rollback is handled if quality dips.
[06:52] Jordan Lee: Will do. Any last questions?
[06:55] Lucia Park: Please send SOC2 and a sample security checklist.
[06:58] Jordan Lee: We'll send both. Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the SOW and benchmark docs.

Meeting end.
